definition: Fetter means to chain or restrain.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fetter. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fetter should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Superstition fettered the whaling crew as surely as any gale: no sailing on Fridays, no whistling on deck, no renaming a boat.
Hobble is gentler than fetter — a hobbled walker still gets there, late and limping; a fettered one drags chains at every step.
Paralyze goes beyond fetter: fettered plans still creep forward, link by link, while paralyzed ones cannot move at all.

A shackle is the literal iron cuff, and to shackle is to lock it on — the word stays close to hardware even in figurative use. Fetter shares the picture of leg irons but ranges more freely: fear, tradition, and habit can all fetter a person, hanging on and dragging at every step.

To encumber is to weigh someone down with baggage or burdens, making every step slower and more awkward. Fetter is harsher and blames the restraint itself: what fetters you chains you like leg irons, and the word carries a blame the neutral load of encumbrance does not.
to take the restraints off entirely
to let go of what was held

Fetter is one of English's own oldest words, not a borrowing: Old English feter named the chain that bound a prisoner's feet, and it grew from the same ancient root as foot. The chain and the foot travel together in the word — which is why fettered things can still shuffle, but never stride.

The marine lab's younger scientists had a joke: the ocean was easy, the paperwork impossible.
Grant rules written decades ago continued to fetter their research, hanging on every project like a chain no one remembered forging.
A simple water sample required three signatures; a new instrument, eleven.
Nothing was outright forbidden.
Work crept forward — but slowly, and with a bitterness the old rules seemed almost designed to produce.
When the director finally struck the worst requirements from the handbook, one biologist swore the whole building stood up straighter.
